blocks.x: SECTION 08 · DIAGRAMS
Diagram Playbook
This tab answers: which diagram should explain this part of the game, and how do I draw it so the team can act on it?

Fill the translation table in 8.2 first, then draw only the diagrams your current milestone needs. Copy a recipe's spec table into the owning GDD tab and replace the example sketch with your own; do not maintain two versions.
8.1 Why game design needs diagrams
Draw only when a list of words has failed to settle a question. Start with the question, then choose the diagram; never start with the tool.

A diagram has two jobs. **Communication** aligns a room: it is drawn fast, argued over, and thrown away when the decision is made. **Documentation** preserves a decision: it is versioned, owned, and cited by engineering, art, and QA. Label every diagram as one or the other. A whiteboard sketch that people treat as a spec is a trap; a polished diagram with no owner is decoration.

One diagram answers one question. How does a player get from boot to gameplay? is a game flow. What can interrupt an attack? is a state machine. What happens in the 120 ms after a hit lands? is a sequence. If you cannot write the question in one sentence, split the diagram. If two questions share a canvas, the reader will answer the easier one and ignore the other.

A table beats a diagram when the content is exact values, a matrix of states and inputs, a schedule, or a checklist. Use a diagram for topology, sequence, flow, dependency, and containment. Use a table for parameters, cooldowns, damage types, spawn counts, and ownership. A state table with 14 states and 6 shared events is easier to verify than a state diagram with 84 arrows.

**Diagram debt** is the gap between the diagram the team trusts and the system that ships. Symptoms: three versions in chat, arrows nobody can explain, a diagram older than the feature it describes, and a newcomer asking which box is real. Pay it down at every milestone: update the source, re-export, or delete the diagram. A stale diagram is worse than no diagram because it teaches the wrong system with confidence.

8.3 Diagram standards
Adopt one legend across the whole GDD before the second diagram exists. A reader who has to relearn your shapes on every page will stop reading the diagrams.

The standards below apply to every diagram in the GDD, including the sketches in this tab. The sketches in 8.4–8.15 are schematics; use the shapes named in each recipe's Elements row, not the ASCII approximations. A diagram that ignores these standards is a conversation, not documentation; label it as such.
Legend and naming

Keep the legend to seven semantic marks: mode or screen, system, state, decision, data entity, pool, and external actor. Shape carries type within one diagram family; the same rectangle can mean system on a systems map and room on a level map, but never both on one canvas. Line style carries timing (solid for immediate or synchronous, dashed for delayed or async). Colour carries one dimension only, player versus system, team, or status, and never the only carrier of meaning. Put the legend on the canvas, bottom-left, at 9 pt or larger.

x: Title as a question: How does a run end? not Run flow v3.
Nodes are nouns from the glossary; arrows are verbs or events.
IDs stay stable across versions; do not rename a node because the layout moved.
File name: dia_[system]_[question]_v[major].[ext]. No final, no copy, no date-only names.
Set ASCII sketches in Roboto Mono 8.5; proportional fonts break alignment.
Footer on every diagram: owner, date, status (draft, review, approved), and source link.

blocks.x: One question, one direction

Write the question above the title. If the diagram needs two sentences to explain its scope, it is two diagrams. Put the scope boundary on the canvas: a dashed box labelled out of scope prevents the reader from inventing connections.

Flow reads left-to-right; hierarchy reads top-to-bottom; time reads left-to-right; cycles read clockwise. Pick one direction per diagram and keep it. If an arrow must cross the flow, use a bridge or a labelled jump, not a diagonal through three boxes. A reader should be able to trace the main path with a finger in under ten seconds.
Colour, version, and source

x: Blue = player action or player-owned data.
Orange = system, server, or simulation.
Red = failure, block, or loss.
Green = reward, unlock, or recovery.
Grey = out of scope, disabled, or deprecated.
Never use colour alone; pair it with a label, shape, or icon.

blocks.x: Version with v1.2, not dates alone. Bump the minor for layout or wording, the major for a change in meaning. Keep the editable source in the project drive or repo next to the GDD; export a PNG for the doc and link the source in the caption. A screenshot pasted from chat is not a source file. When a diagram changes meaning, archive the old export instead of overwriting it.
Alt text and quick review

Write alt text as the takeaway plus the structure: The run ends in one of three ways: extraction, death, or timeout; death is the only path that loses meta-currency. Two sentences maximum. Do not describe every box; describe what the reader must know if the image fails to load.

8.4 Game flow / mode map
Use a game flow when a player, a producer, or QA cannot agree on how a mode is entered, exited, or recovered. Draw modes, not menu widgets.

head: Field
Spec
rows: Which modes exist, and what event moves the player between them?
Rounded rectangle = mode; diamond = branch; solid arrow = player action; dashed arrow = automatic transition; label = event plus condition; double outline = terminal.

1 List modes from boot to quit, including pause, death, disconnect, and error. 2 Put the happy path on one horizontal spine. 3 Add branches above or below, never on top. 4 Label every arrow with its event. 5 Mark transitions that save, load, or reset state.
Mixing screens with modes; omitting pause, death, and network-loss exits; labelling arrows next; hiding three modes in one box.
FigJam or Miro for the workshop; draw.io for the approved export.

8.5 Core loop (nested loops)
Use a core loop when the pitch says the loop is fun but nobody can name the three verbs the player repeats. Draw the loop at three time scales before writing a feature list.

head: Field
Spec
rows: What does the player repeat at each time scale, and how does the short loop feed the long one?
Outer frame = session; middle frame = route or encounter; inner frame = action; verb nodes; reward nodes; arrow = causal link; annotation = duration and repeat count.

1 Write the 30-second loop as 3–5 verbs with input and feedback. 2 Wrap it in the 5-minute loop that gives the reward a use. 3 Wrap that in the session loop that changes the plan. 4 Draw one arrow from each reward to the next decision it enables. 5 Put a duration on every frame.
A linear tutorial drawn as a loop; a reward with no sink; only one time scale; a last step that does not change the first.
Paper first; FigJam for the shared version; Miro for a group teardown.

8.6 State machine (player, AI, session)
Use a state machine when behaviour depends on what happened before, or when a bug report says the enemy got stuck. Draw one entity per diagram.

head: Field
Spec
rows: What states can this entity be in, what event moves it, and what does it do on entry?

Rounded rectangle = state (noun); arrow = transition labelled event [guard] / action; black dot = start; double circle = end; self-loop = repeat; composite box = nested state; dashed arrow = interrupt.

1 List states as nouns or adjectives, never verbs. 2 Name the event that exits each state, including timeout and cancel. 3 Add guards where one event has different outcomes. 4 Put entry and exit actions inside the box. 5 Check every state has an exit and every event has a home.
Attacking as a state when it is an action; no interrupt priority; booleans that duplicate states; transitions with no event.

8.7 Activity / quest flowchart
Use a quest flowchart when a quest has branches, parallel objectives, fail states, or more than one way to complete it. If it is a straight line, write a numbered list instead.

head: Field
Spec
rows: What must the player do, in what order, and where can the quest fail or branch?
Rounded rectangle = player objective; diamond = condition; bar = fork/join; swimlane = owner; note = fail or retry; solid arrow = required step; dashed arrow = optional.

1 Start from the completion condition and work backwards. 2 Write objectives in player language, not UI language. 3 Add a diamond for every condition that can send the player back. 4 Show fail, abandon, and retry. 5 Join parallel objectives with a bar.
Flowcharts of menu clicks; diamonds with one exit; no failure path; parallel objectives that never join; no already-completed state.

8.8 Sequence / interaction timing
Use a sequence diagram when the argument is about order or timing: input latency, server authority, hit feedback, or who owns a state change. Do not use it to show content flow.

head: Field
Spec
rows: In what order do input, authority, feedback, and audio fire, and how far apart?
Lifeline per participant; solid arrow = request; dashed arrow = return; filled head = synchronous; open head = async; activation bar = processing; time note = budget in ms.

1 Name the trigger and the observable result. 2 List only participants that touch that result. 3 Put time left-to-right and number each message. 4 Mark who has authority and the feedback deadline. 5 Annotate the budget per step.
Mixing client and server on one lifeline; no returns; internal calls the player never sees; feedback before confirmation; no timeout path.
FigJam or Miro sequence plugin; PlantUML or Mermaid for a versioned source.
{{02 Gameplay & Systems}} → interaction spec; {{06 Technical Design}} → timing budget.

8.9 Systems map / dependency graph
Use a systems map when a change in one system keeps breaking another, or when the team cannot agree on what is core. Map dependencies, not classes.

head: Field
Spec
rows: Which systems depend on which, and where will a change cascade?
Rectangle = system (one noun); arrow = dependency labelled reads, writes, owns, or triggers; solid = synchronous; dashed = event or async; colour = layer; dashed boundary = scope.

1 List 8–15 systems at one abstraction level. 2 Draw arrows from the owner of data to the reader. 3 Label the payload or event, not uses. 4 Circle the top three fan-in nodes and name an owner. 5 Box the slice you will build first.
One node per class; arrows with no direction; mixing runtime and build dependencies; no async legend; an org chart in disguise.
Miro or Obsidian Canvas for discovery; draw.io for the approved map.

Use a class or entity model before schema, save format, or content tooling work. Draw the data the game must persist, not every object in code.

8.11 Economy flow (faucets, sinks, pools, converters)
Use an economy flow when players have too much or too little of something, or when a new source or sink is proposed. One resource per diagram; convert later.

head: Field
Spec
rows: Where does each resource enter, where does it pool, what converts it, and where does it leave?

Circle = pool; inbound arrow = faucet; downward triangle = sink; triangle with line = converter; diamond = gate or chance; solid arrow = flow with rate; dashed arrow = state connection; colour per resource.

1 Pick one resource and one time unit. 2 Put faucets left, pools centre, sinks right. 3 Label every arrow with amount and cadence. 4 Add converters where one resource becomes another. 5 Compare inflow and outflow at target playtime.
No time unit; faucets without sinks; uncapped pools; converters that create net value; tuning by feel.
Machinations for simulation; a spreadsheet for the numbers; Miro for the first sketch.

8.12 Level flow / beat chart (map + pacing curve)
Use a level flow and beat chart when a level feels flat, exhausting, or confusing, or when a reviewer asks what the player learns and when. Draw the map and the intensity curve on the same page.

head: Field
Spec
rows: What is the critical path through the level, and how does intensity rise and fall along it?
Rectangle = room or beat; thick arrow = critical path; thin dashed = optional; diamond = gate; chart x = time or order, y = intensity 0–10; label = duration, teaching goal, encounter type.

1 Draw the critical path left to right. 2 Add optional rooms below the spine. 3 Number beats in play order. 4 Plot the same beats on a 0–10 intensity curve. 5 Mark the teaching beat and the peak; justify a peak that is not the finale.
A map with no durations; a curve with no beat labels; every beat at 8/10; no rest after a peak; secrets that break pacing.
Paper for the map; Figma or Miro for the beat chart; a spreadsheet for durations.

8.13 Narrative branch graph
Use a narrative branch graph when choices change scenes, flags, or endings, and the writer needs to see the cost of each branch. If the story is linear, use a beat sheet.

head: Field
Spec
rows: Where does the story branch, what choice causes it, and where do branches reconverge?
Rectangle = scene or passage; diamond = choice point; arrow = choice labelled with a verb; colour = act; flag note = variable set; double outline = ending; dashed = conditional shortcut.

1 List the endings and work backwards to the last common scene. 2 Put the choice on the edge, not in the node. 3 Mark flags set and tested. 4 Fold reconverging branches into a hub. 5 Count scenes per ending and mark the cheapest and most expensive path.
Every choice creates an ending; no reconvergence; flags with no visible test; a hairball; no word budget per branch.
Twine for structure and playtest; Ink for shipped text; Obsidian Canvas for lore links.

8.14 Progression / unlock graph
Use a progression graph when unlocks gate content, and the team needs to see the critical path and the optional power. Draw what opens what, not the UI tree.

head: Field
Spec
rows: What can the player unlock, what does it open, and what is the critical path?
Rectangle = unlock; hexagon or diamond = gate; arrow = requires; thick arrow = critical path; thin = optional; label = cost and prerequisite; colour = tier.

1 List unlocks in intended order. 2 Put each gate after the unlock that opens it. 3 Draw the critical path as a straight spine. 4 Add optional branches with costs. 5 Check every gate has a visible key before it is needed.
A linear chain labelled as a graph; gates with no in-world tell; optional rewards that trivialize the spine; no cost; duplicate keys with no reason.
